title: Are Your Class Rules Enforceable?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on a previous exercise, Linsin explains a subtle problem some readers discovered: rules that don't actually cover any real disruptions because they're really encouragements — vague, unenforceable aspirations like 'do your best' or 'be a friend' that are commonly mistaken for rules. He argues real rules exist solely to protect the teacher's freedom to teach and students' right to learn, and must be specific enough to be enforced consistently. Encouragements, by contrast, are confusing to students and can be hurtful if a teacher tries to enforce them as though they were rules. He recommends readers revisit last week's exercise, discard any items that turn out to be encouragements rather than enforceable rules, and keep encouragements only as themes or reminders.
points: Identifies a common error: mistaking vague 'encouragements' (e.g., 'do your best,' 'be a friend') for enforceable class rules.
Argues that true rules exist solely to protect the freedom to teach and the right to learn, focused narrowly on curbing disruptions.
Notes encouragements are vague, subjective, and nearly impossible to enforce consistently or fairly.
Warns that attempting to enforce encouragements as rules is confusing and can be hurtful to students.
Recommends keeping encouragements only as classroom themes or reminders, not as part of the enforceable rule set.
quotes: It’s common to confuse rules with encouragements—which are behaviors you’d like to see in your students but are ultimately unenforceable.
Do your best. Be ready to learn. Try new things. Have fun. Dream big. Make wise choices.
Rules protect your freedom to teach and your students’ right to learn and enjoy school. That’s it.
Encouragements like those listed above, on the other hand, do no such thing and are all but impossible to enforce.
They’re also incredibly confusing to students—and hurtful if you do attempt to enforce them.
Some readers even discovered that none of their rules covered actual disruptions.
